name: Deep-Water Wave Phase Speed
description: Gives the phase speed of a deep-water surface gravity wave, g*T/(2*pi), from its period T. In deep water longer-period waves travel faster, so speed increases linearly with period.
notes: Valid only in deep water (depth greater than about half the wavelength). It is the crest (phase) speed, twice the energy-carrying group velocity for these waves.

name: Shallow-Water Wave Speed
description: Returns the speed sqrt(g*h) of a long wave in shallow water, depending only on depth h. It applies to tsunamis, tides, and long swells whose wavelength greatly exceeds the water depth.
notes: Valid only in the shallow-water (long-wave) limit, wavelength much larger than depth. Non-dispersive: all such waves travel at this same depth-set speed.

name: Airy Wave Phase Speed (Finite Depth)
description: Computes the linear (Airy) surface-wave phase speed at finite depth, sqrt((g/k)*tanh(k*h)) expressed with exponentials. It smoothly bridges the deep-water and shallow-water limits as the depth-to-wavelength ratio changes.
notes: k is the wavenumber (2*pi/L) in 1/m; the exponential form equals (g/k)*tanh(k*h). For large k*h it approaches deep-water speed, for small k*h shallow-water speed.

name: Deep-Water Group Velocity
description: Gives the group velocity g*T/(4*pi) of deep-water surface waves, the speed at which wave energy and the wave-group envelope propagate. It is exactly half the phase (crest) speed in deep water.
notes: Valid in deep water only. Because it is half the phase speed, individual crests appear to advance through and vanish at the front of a wave group.

name: Deep-Water Dispersion Frequency
description: Returns the angular frequency sqrt(g*k) of a deep-water surface gravity wave from its wavenumber k. This is the linear dispersion relation, showing that shorter waves (larger k) oscillate faster.
notes: k is wavenumber (2*pi/L) in 1/m and the result is angular frequency in rad/s (divide by 2*pi for hertz). Valid in the deep-water limit only.

name: Wave Energy Density
description: Computes the mean total (kinetic plus potential) energy per unit sea-surface area of a linear wave, (1/8)*rho*g*H^2. Energy scales with the square of wave height H, so doubling height quadruples energy.
notes: H is wave height (crest to trough), not amplitude; use amplitude a=H/2 with (1/2)*rho*g*a^2 for the equivalent form. rho is seawater density.

name: Deep-Water Wave Power
description: Estimates the energy flux (power) per unit crest width carried by deep-water waves, rho*g^2*H^2*T/(64*pi). Power grows with the square of wave height and linearly with period, making long high swells energy-rich.
notes: Result is power per metre of wave crest (W/m). H is wave height (crest to trough) and T the period; valid in deep water using the linear-wave approximation.

name: Significant Wave Height from Spectrum
description: Computes the significant wave height as 4*sqrt(m0), where m0 is the zeroth spectral moment (the variance of the sea-surface elevation). This spectral definition (Hm0) approximates the average height of the highest one-third of waves.
notes: m0 is the total variance in m^2 (area under the wave spectrum). Hm0 closely matches, but is not identical to, the time-domain significant height H1/3.

name: Surface Stokes Drift Velocity
description: Gives the surface Stokes drift velocity pi^2*H^2/(T*L) of a linear deep-water wave, the small net forward transport of water experienced by a floating particle over each wave cycle even though the wave itself carries no mean current.
notes: This is the surface value; drift decays rapidly with depth. Uses wave height H, period T, and wavelength L, which are linked by the dispersion relation.

name: Wave Steepness
description: Returns the wave steepness H/L, the ratio of wave height to wavelength. This dimensionless number indicates how peaked a wave is and how close it is to breaking.
notes: Dimensionless. Deep-water waves break when steepness reaches about 1/7 (0.142); higher computed values are physically unrealistic for a stable wave.

name: Ursell Number
description: Computes the Ursell number H*L^2/h^3, which measures the degree of nonlinearity of surface waves in water of depth h. Small values justify linear (Airy) theory, large values call for nonlinear (cnoidal) theory.
notes: Dimensionless; H is wave height, L wavelength, h depth. Roughly, values below about 40 allow linear theory; above that shallow-water nonlinear effects matter.

name: Iribarren Number
description: Gives the Iribarren number (surf similarity parameter) tan(beta)/sqrt(H/L), combining beach slope beta with wave steepness. It classifies how waves break on a slope: spilling, plunging, or surging.
notes: beta is the beach slope angle in radians; H and L are the incident wave height and wavelength (often deep-water values). Low values give spilling breakers, high values surging.

name: Coriolis Acceleration
description: Computes the horizontal Coriolis acceleration 2*Omega*v*sin(phi) acting on a mass moving at speed v at latitude phi due to Earth's rotation. It deflects moving fluids and objects, rightward in the northern hemisphere.
notes: phi is latitude in radians and Omega Earth's rotation rate; the effect vanishes at the equator (sin 0) and peaks at the poles. This gives the acceleration magnitude, not direction.

name: Inertial Oscillation Period
description: Returns the inertial oscillation period pi/(Omega*sin(phi)), the time for a free-moving parcel in a rotating ocean to complete one inertial circle at latitude phi. It equals half a pendulum day.
notes: phi is latitude in radians; the period lengthens toward the equator and diverges there (sin approaches 0). Equal to pi/f with the Coriolis parameter f=2*Omega*sin(phi).

name: Barotropic Rossby Radius
description: Computes the barotropic Rossby radius of deformation sqrt(g*H)/f, the length scale where rotation and gravity balance for depth-averaged ocean flow. It sets the size of large-scale currents and eddies influenced by Earth's rotation.
notes: H is the full ocean depth and f the Coriolis parameter (about 1e-4 s^-1 at mid-latitudes). Distinct from the baroclinic radius, which uses reduced gravity and is much smaller.

name: Brunt-Vaisala Frequency
description: Gives the Brunt-Vaisala (buoyancy) frequency sqrt((g/rho)*drho), the natural angular frequency at which a vertically displaced fluid parcel oscillates in a stably stratified fluid. Stronger density stratification gives faster oscillations.
notes: drho is the vertical density gradient magnitude for stable stratification (density increasing downward). A negative gradient means instability and no real frequency (the root fails).

name: Brunt-Vaisala Period
description: Returns the buoyancy oscillation period 2*pi/N from the Brunt-Vaisala frequency N. It is the time for one full buoyancy oscillation of a displaced parcel in a stratified fluid, longer where stratification is weaker.
notes: N is the buoyancy frequency in rad/s; the result is in seconds. Simply the inverse relation to frequency, so a small N gives a very long period.

name: Geostrophic Current Velocity
description: Computes the geostrophic current speed (g/f)*slope from the sea surface slope, the balance between the horizontal pressure-gradient force and the Coriolis force. It gives the large-scale ocean current implied by a tilted sea surface.
notes: slope is the dimensionless sea-surface gradient and f the Coriolis parameter. Valid for steady, large-scale, frictionless flow away from the equator (where f approaches 0).

name: Reduced Gravity
description: Returns the reduced gravity g*drho/rho, the effective buoyant acceleration felt at the interface between two fluid layers of small density difference drho. It replaces full gravity in stratified-flow and internal-wave problems.
notes: drho is the density difference between layers and rho a reference density; the result is much smaller than g. Assumes the Boussinesq approximation (small relative density difference).

name: Two-Layer Internal Wave Speed
description: Computes the phase speed sqrt(gr*h1*h2/(h1+h2)) of a long internal wave along the interface of a two-layer stratified fluid. It uses the reduced gravity gr and the two layer depths h1 and h2.
notes: gr is the reduced gravity (much less than g), so internal waves are far slower than surface waves. Valid in the long-wave limit for two well-mixed layers.

name: Densimetric Froude Number
description: Returns the densimetric (internal) Froude number u/sqrt(gr*h), comparing the flow speed u to the internal wave speed set by reduced gravity gr and layer depth h. It indicates whether a stratified flow is sub- or supercritical.
notes: gr is reduced gravity, not full gravity; using g would greatly underestimate the number. Values above 1 mean the flow outruns internal waves (supercritical).

name: Ekman Transport (Volume)
description: Computes the wind-driven Ekman volume transport per unit width of the ocean surface layer, obtained by dividing the wind stress by the product of seawater density and the Coriolis parameter. The result is a depth-integrated horizontal transport directed perpendicular to the wind.
notes: The net Ekman transport is 90 degrees to the right of the wind in the Northern Hemisphere (left in the Southern). Fails near the equator where the Coriolis parameter f approaches zero.

name: Ekman Layer Depth
description: Estimates the depth of the wind-driven Ekman layer, defined as pi times the square root of twice the vertical eddy viscosity divided by the Coriolis parameter. It marks the depth at which the wind-driven current has rotated fully and decayed to a small fraction of its surface value.
notes: Assumes a constant vertical eddy viscosity, which is a strong idealization. Depth grows toward low latitudes as f shrinks and is undefined at the equator.

name: Sverdrup Transport
description: Calculates the meridional (north-south) depth-integrated ocean transport per unit width driven by the curl of the wind stress, via the Sverdrup balance. It is the wind stress curl divided by the product of density and the beta parameter (the meridional gradient of the Coriolis parameter).
notes: Valid for the ocean interior away from western boundary currents. A positive wind stress curl drives poleward transport; sign conventions must be applied consistently.

name: Mackenzie Seawater Sound Speed
description: Gives the speed of sound in seawater using Mackenzie's nine-term empirical polynomial in temperature, salinity, and depth. It captures how sound velocity increases with warmer water, higher salinity, and greater depth (pressure).
notes: Valid roughly for 2 to 30 degrees C, salinity 25 to 40 psu, and depth 0 to 8000 m. Uses depth in metres, not pressure; salinity terms are referenced to 35 psu.

name: Seawater Freezing Point
description: Computes the freezing temperature of seawater as a function of salinity and pressure using the standard UNESCO polynomial. Higher salinity and greater pressure both lower the freezing point below 0 degrees C.
notes: Salinity is in practical salinity units and pressure in decibars (gauge, zero at the surface). The result is negative for typical ocean salinities.

name: Linear Seawater Density (Equation of State)
description: Approximates seawater density using a linearized equation of state, where density departs from a reference value in proportion to temperature and salinity anomalies. Warming (via the thermal expansion coefficient) lowers density and increased salinity (via the haline contraction coefficient) raises it.
notes: A local linearization valid only for small anomalies about the reference state; it omits pressure and the nonlinearity of the real equation of state.

name: Steric Sea-Level Rise (Thermal Expansion)
description: Estimates the steric (thermal expansion) rise in sea level of a water column, given by the product of the thermal expansion coefficient, the column depth, and the temperature increase. It represents the expansion of ocean water as it warms.
notes: Assumes a uniform temperature rise and a constant expansion coefficient over the column; the real coefficient varies strongly with temperature and pressure. Excludes salinity (halosteric) effects.

name: Wind Stress (Bulk Formula)
description: Computes the wind stress on the sea surface using the bulk aerodynamic formula: air density times the drag coefficient times the square of the wind speed. It gives the momentum flux from wind into the ocean per unit area.
notes: Wind speed should be referenced to a standard height, typically 10 m. The drag coefficient itself depends on wind speed and stability, so a fixed value is an approximation.

name: Pierson-Moskowitz Significant Height
description: Gives the significant wave height of a fully developed sea from the Pierson-Moskowitz spectrum, equal to 0.21 times the wind speed squared divided by gravitational acceleration. It represents the equilibrium wave height reached when wind blows steadily over unlimited fetch and duration.
notes: Wind speed is referenced to 19.5 m height as in the original formulation. Applies only to a fully developed sea, not fetch- or duration-limited conditions.

name: Pierson-Moskowitz Peak Period
description: Computes the peak spectral wave period of a fully developed sea, given by 2 pi times the wind speed divided by 0.877 times gravity. It is the period of the dominant waves at spectral equilibrium.
notes: Valid only for a fully developed sea; the constant 0.877 sets the peak frequency of the Pierson-Moskowitz spectrum. Use a consistent reference height for the wind speed.

name: Fetch-Limited Significant Wave Height
description: Estimates the significant wave height for a fetch-limited sea, where wave growth is bounded by the over-water distance (fetch) rather than time. It scales with the wind speed and the square root of the product of gravity and fetch.
notes: Applies when duration is ample but fetch limits growth; valid below the fully developed limit. Fetch and wind speed must use consistent SI units.

name: Fetch-Limited Peak Period
description: Estimates the peak wave period for a fetch-limited sea, growing with the dimensionless fetch (g F over U squared) raised to about the one-third power. Longer fetch produces longer-period dominant waves.
notes: Uses empirical growth-law constants valid only below the fully developed sea; the period saturates once the sea is fully developed. Keep fetch and wind in consistent units.

name: Wave Shoaling Coefficient
description: Gives the shoaling coefficient describing how wave height changes as a wave moves into shallower water, equal to the square root of the ratio of deep-water to local group velocity. A value above one means the wave grows in height as it shoals.
notes: Accounts for energy conservation from shoaling alone, ignoring refraction, reflection, and breaking. Multiply by the incident height to obtain the local wave height.

name: Wave Refraction Angle (Snell)
description: Computes the refracted wave direction as ocean waves cross a boundary between regions of different phase speed, using Snell's law for water waves. The refracted angle bends toward the region of slower wave speed (shallower water).
notes: Angles are in radians measured from the normal to the depth contours. Total reflection occurs if the argument of asin exceeds one, which the formula does not guard against.

name: Breaking Wave Depth
description: Estimates the water depth at which a wave of a given breaking height breaks, obtained by dividing the breaking wave height by the breaker index (depth-limited breaking ratio). It marks the onset of surf-zone breaking.
notes: The breaker index gamma_b is typically about 0.78 for gently sloping beaches but varies with slope and wave steepness. Assumes depth-limited breaking.

name: Deep-Water Orbital Velocity
description: Gives the maximum orbital velocity of water particles at the surface of a deep-water wave, equal to pi times the wave height divided by the wave period. It represents the peak speed of the circular particle motion.
notes: Valid only in deep water where orbits are circular and the depth exceeds about half the wavelength; velocity decays exponentially with depth.

name: Tsunami Propagation Speed
description: Computes the propagation speed of a tsunami as a shallow-water (long) wave, equal to the square root of gravity times the ocean depth. Deeper water yields faster tsunami travel, reaching hundreds of metres per second in the open ocean.
notes: Valid in the shallow-water limit where wavelength greatly exceeds depth, which holds for tsunamis; speed is independent of wave height or period.

name: Green's Law Wave Height
description: Predicts the change in wave height as a long wave travels from deep to shallow water using Green's law, scaling with the fourth root of the depth ratio. As depth decreases, the wave height increases.
notes: Valid for shallow-water (long) waves over a gently varying bottom, accounting only for shoaling. Ignores refraction, friction, and breaking near shore.

name: Munk Boundary Layer Width
description: Estimates the width of the Munk western boundary layer, set by lateral (horizontal) friction, as the cube root of the horizontal eddy viscosity divided by the beta parameter. It characterizes the scale of viscous western boundary currents.
notes: Applies to the frictional western boundary layer where horizontal eddy viscosity balances the beta effect; the value is sensitive to the assumed eddy viscosity.

name: Stommel Boundary Layer Width
description: Estimates the width of the Stommel western boundary layer, controlled by bottom friction, as the bottom friction coefficient divided by the beta parameter. It sets the scale over which the western boundary current adjusts.
notes: Applies to the bottom-friction western boundary layer; contrast with the Munk layer governed by lateral friction. The result is a horizontal length scale in metres.

name: Thermal Wind Shear
description: Computes the vertical shear of the geostrophic current from a horizontal density gradient via the thermal wind balance. It equals minus gravity over (Coriolis parameter times density) multiplied by the horizontal density gradient, linking horizontal density structure to how current changes with depth.
notes: This gives one component of the vertical shear per unit depth. Fails near the equator where f vanishes; sign depends on the orientation of the density gradient.

name: Wave Age
description: Gives the dimensionless wave age, the ratio of wave phase speed to wind speed. Young seas have small wave age (waves slower than the wind), while values near or above one indicate mature or swell-dominated seas.
notes: Both speeds should be defined consistently, with wind speed referenced to a standard height. Values above one mean waves outrun the local wind.

name: Wedderburn Number
description: Computes the dimensionless Wedderburn number characterizing the tilt of a lake or ocean pycnocline under wind forcing. It is reduced gravity times the squared mixed-layer depth divided by the squared water friction velocity times the basin length.
notes: Large values indicate a stable, level interface; values near or below one signal strong tilting and possible upwelling of the interface at the upwind end.

name: Gradient Richardson Number (Ocean)
description: Gives the gradient Richardson number, the ratio of the buoyancy frequency squared to the squared vertical velocity shear. It measures whether stratification (stability) or shear (instability) dominates in the water column.
notes: Values below about 0.25 indicate the flow is prone to shear instability and turbulent mixing; large values indicate strong stability that suppresses mixing.

name: Beta-Plane Parameter
description: Computes the beta parameter, the northward gradient of the Coriolis parameter, as twice the Earth's rotation rate times the cosine of latitude divided by the Earth's radius. It quantifies how the Coriolis effect strengthens with latitude.
notes: Latitude is in radians. Beta is largest at the equator and vanishes at the poles; it underpins the beta-plane approximation used in geophysical fluid dynamics.

name: Rhines Scale
description: Computes the Rhines scale, the length at which turbulent eddies give way to Rossby waves, equal to the square root of an eddy velocity scale divided by the beta parameter. It marks the transition from isotropic turbulence to zonal jet formation.
notes: Uses a representative eddy velocity; the result is a horizontal length scale in metres. It grows with stronger eddies and smaller beta (higher latitudes).

name: Ocean Buoyancy Flux
description: Computes the surface buoyancy flux driven by heat exchange, equal to gravity times the thermal expansion coefficient times the surface heat flux, divided by density times specific heat. It converts a heat flux into an equivalent buoyancy forcing of the surface layer.
notes: This form accounts only for the thermal (heat) contribution, omitting freshwater (salinity) buoyancy fluxes. A cooling (negative Q) produces a destabilizing buoyancy loss.

name: Ekman Pumping Velocity
description: Computes the vertical Ekman pumping velocity at the base of the surface Ekman layer, given by the wind stress curl divided by density times the Coriolis parameter. Positive values indicate upward pumping (upwelling) driven by wind stress curl.
notes: Sign depends on the hemisphere and curl convention; a positive curl drives upwelling in the Northern Hemisphere. Undefined at the equator where f approaches zero.
